analysis:
Examined the onboarding flow and follower changes. The PR adds a stop-count mechanism: `stopsAsked` and `serveUnlessStopped` operations, `stopsBefore` threaded through start, wait, provision and move, and `endsOnStopAsked`. It also adds a `ClusterOnboardingLooker` that polls at most once a second. In the follower (ClusterOnboardingFollow.swift, head ~201-204 and ~276-284), it replaces the status-text heuristic (a Stopped status held 20 s) with `ClusterOnboardingFollowedStop.look(look.stopsAsked, ...)`, a count-based stop detector.

Security relevance is limited to local UX and control flow for cluster onboarding. No changes touch the key, attestation, encryption or authorization boundaries (TB-002, TB-009, TB-011, A-016). The stop signal is a counter read over the cable from the paired Mac, which is the same trust domain as the previous status text. A malicious peer could already end the follower's wait by publishing a Stopped status, so this adds no new capability. If the peer reports an inflated count, it ends only the local follower's wait, a DoS on the local UX at most. Nil from an older build falls back to no stop detection, which is fail-safe for availability.

The Looker spawns at most one detached thread per second, with one look in flight at a time, so thread growth is bounded. `ClusterOnboardingMailbox` is lock-protected.

The unseen code needing integration review is `ClusterOnboardingFollowedStop` and the live `stopsAsked` / `serveUnlessStopped` implementations in `OnboardingLive` and `ClusterSetupRecord`. The questions are whether the stop count is correctly authenticated, whether `serveUnlessStopped` is race-free, and whether the lock prevents a stale start from undoing a stop. The pair-wire authentication that carries `stopsAsked` is also outside the supplied evidence. No concrete regression is visible in the supplied lines.
